title: How Homelessness Works
summary: Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant discuss homelessness in the United States, opening with Facebook page banter and a reference to a blog post Chuck wrote on rising homeless school children (a 41 percent national increase, with Texas and Iowa among the highest). They cover worldwide and US counts (point-in-time counts versus annual Census-based estimates, shelter bed numbers, and minority overrepresentation), then causes: poverty, the gap between minimum wage and the poverty line and affordable housing, the demolition of low-rent housing and cuts to housing assistance from 1980 to 2003, mental illness including the claim about Reagan-era closures of mental hospitals, addiction, domestic violence, and veterans. They discuss the McKinney-Vento Act, effects on homeless people (physical attacks, health problems, PTSD), programs such as Section 8 vouchers, shelters, public housing, food banks and food waste, and job training. They close with ways listeners can help and a call to see homeless people as individuals. The episode ends with a listener mail segment about Kiva microloans, a Kiva team listing, and a holiday story request.

segments.title: Opening banter and homeless school children
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with Facebook page chatter, then Chuck introduces the July news about rising numbers of homeless school children, citing a 41 percent national increase and large jumps in Texas, Iowa and Sioux Falls.

segments.title: Counting the homeless worldwide and in the US
segments.summary: The hosts explain point-in-time counts versus annual Census-based estimates and why counts are hard. They cite worldwide figures, note homelessness in Sweden and Norway, and give conflicting US totals. They also note disproportionate homelessness among minorities, especially African Americans, and that families make up a large share of rural homelessness.

segments.title: Defining homelessness and its history
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck explain that homelessness includes people without a permanent residence, such as those in weekly motels or staying with family, not just people on the street. They mention historical vagrancy laws in fourteenth-century England and say homelessness has existed in the US since its founding.

segments.title: Poverty, minimum wage and affordable housing
segments.summary: The hosts describe the poverty line, the federal minimum wage of 7.25 an hour, and the gap that makes full-time minimum-wage work fall below poverty. They explain that affordable housing is defined as 30 percent of income and that about five million US households pay more than half their income in rent. Many homeless people hold jobs, and job loss, medical bills or catastrophe can push ordinary people into homelessness.

segments.title: Demolition of low-rent housing and cuts to assistance
segments.summary: Chuck and Josh discuss the demolition of Techwood Homes in Atlanta before the Olympics and a nationwide trend in which more than two million low-rent units were demolished or converted between 1980 and 2003, while government housing assistance fell by half in the same period.

segments.title: Mental illness, Reagan and addiction
segments.summary: The hosts say about 20 percent of homeless people have a mental illness and about two-thirds struggle with alcohol or drug problems. They discuss the urban legend that Reagan closed mental institutions, which they say is largely accurate: he cut state psychiatric hospitals as California governor and cut mental health treatment funding as president.

segments.title: McKinney-Vento Act and domestic violence
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the McKinney-Vento Act, signed by Reagan and named for Stewart McKinney and Bruce Vento, which funded shelters, transitional housing, healthcare, food and job training. They then cover domestic violence as a cause of homelessness, with about half of homeless women described as battered women, and the abuse homeless people face on the street.

segments.title: Veterans and the cycle of homelessness
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck discuss homeless veterans, about 200,000 homeless single men, often with PTSD or substance abuse. They describe a vicious cycle in which mental illness, addiction and scarce services reinforce each other, and they note the Department of Veterans Affairs can serve only part of the homeless veteran population. They argue the money exists but the will is lacking.

segments.title: Health effects and Section 8 housing
segments.summary: The hosts list health effects of homelessness for adults and children, including asthma, infections, depression, anxiety, PTSD, frostbite, HIV and diabetes. They then describe Section 8 vouchers, where tenants pay about 30 percent of rent and the government pays the rest, and note long waiting lists and closed lists in some cities.
topics: stress and PTSD in homeless children

segments.title: Shelters, food banks, job training and how to help
segments.summary: The hosts discuss shelters, public housing, food banks and food waste, with estimates that up to half of US food is thrown away. They cover job training groups such as the Coalition for the Homeless and the Homeless Veterans Reintegration Program. They suggest ways to help: volunteering, donating goods, car donation, advocacy and hiring homeless people. They end with a call to treat homeless people as individuals, referencing Will Smith's film and David Pearle's story and photography projects Shelter and Invisible Families.

segments.title: Closing remarks
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck wrap up the homelessness discussion and point listeners to the website search bar for more on the topic.
